title: Utilizing 4D-STEM to Elucidate the Impact of DIGM Zones on Corrosion Resistance in Ni-Cr Alloys Exposed to Extreme Environments
content: Corrosion of alloys is a serious challenge for the long-term durability of materials in the extreme environments of advanced nuclear reactors. While Ni-Cr alloys initially self-passivate, high operating temperature (300-400°C) and applied stress can lead to latent intergranular oxidation and cracking. Corresponding selective oxidation of Cr and accelerated grain boundary diffusion can result in diffusion induced grain boundary migration (DIGM), which is accompanied by wave like Cr depletion and Ni enrichment chemical profiles extending 100s of nm below the alloy surface or ahead of crack tips [1, 2]. Previous research has shown that the rupture of surface oxides can also result in continued oxidation through DIGM zones, increasing the risk of mechanical embrittlement and stress corrosion cracking [3]. However, the specific mechanisms regarding how DIGM zones enhance the degradation of grain boundaries during oxidation attacks remains unclear. To understand how these DIGM zones impact Ni-Cr alloys that have undergone exposure to high temperature corrosive environments, we utilize 4D scanning transmission electron microscopy (4D-STEM) to obtain site specific structural information across DIGM affected grain boundaries and at DIGM affected crack tips. By coupling 4D-STEM measurements with elemental analyses from energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS), we correlate structural and compositional changes within the DIGM-zone.
